title: Yakuza: From Samurai to Slot Machines
summary: Josh and Chuck (with guest producer Matt) explain the Japanese yakuza: its origins in masterless samurai (kabuki mono) and 18th-century gamblers and peddlers (bakuto and tekiya), the name derived from the losing hand "ya-ku-za" in the card game oicho-kabu, clan structure (Yamaguchi-gumi, kumicho, oyabun-kobun relationship), initiation and penance (yubitsume finger cutting), Korean members, women in the organization (Fumiko Taka), rackets and legitimate business, notable incidents (2007 Nagasaki mayor shooting), Yakuza in pop culture films, anti-organized-crime laws, and Japan's gun violence statistics. The episode closes with a listener video-blog email and social media plugs.

segments.title: Opening banter and Simpsons yakuza comparison
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners, welcome guest producer Matt, and open with a discussion of a Simpsons episode where Marge's pretzel business ends in a standoff with the mob and the yakuza, then compare yakuza to the mafia.

segments.title: Origins: masterless samurai and outsider status
segments.summary: The yakuza's origins are traced to masterless samurai (kabuki mono) after the samurai lost their role, and to 18th-century gamblers and peddlers (bakuto and tekiya). Hosts note clans claim noble Robin Hood-style origins, which they consider inflated.

segments.title: Name origin from oicho-kabu
segments.summary: The name yakuza comes from the losing hand 8-9-3 (ya-ku-za) in the card game oicho-kabu, meaning worthless, reinforcing the outsider identity. The police term yakuza-dan/bōryokudan is described as a degenerate gangster insult.

segments.title: Clans, hierarchy and oyabun-kobun structure
segments.summary: Yakuza are organized as single clans or confederations; Yamaguchi-gumi is the largest, with about 80,000 members, led by a kumicho in a pyramid structure. The oyabun-kobun relationship is a father-son style mentorship, and the ceremony uses sake cups.

segments.title: Guns, violence and extortion in Japan
segments.summary: Hosts compare Japanese and US gun statistics and note that most gun deaths in Japan are attributed to yakuza. Extortion often relies on politeness and implied threat, such as pressure to make charity donations.

segments.title: Korean members
segments.summary: Koreans make up about ten percent of the yakuza despite being about 0.5 percent of Japan's population, due to discrimination that pushes them to the outsider group and because of smuggling links between Korea and Japan.

segments.title: Women in the yakuza and Fumiko Taka
segments.summary: Women are marginalized in the yakuza, with one exception: Fumiko Taka, wife of Kazuo Taoka, who became the first woman oyabun after his death in the early 1980s and held power for a few months.

segments.title: Yubitsume finger cutting penance
segments.summary: Hosts describe the practice of yubitsume, in which a member who disappoints the oyabun cuts part of a pinky finger as an apology, with further sections removed for repeated mistakes.

segments.title: Rackets, legitimate business and 2007 Nagasaki shooting
segments.summary: Yakuza rackets include gambling, prostitution, smuggling, firearms, pornography and protection fees, and they move into legitimate business such as the stock market and pro wrestling. In 2007 a yakuza-affiliated man shot the mayor of Nagasaki after a dispute over a car damaged at a public works site.

segments.title: Yoshio Kodama, politics, laws and pop culture
segments.summary: Yoshio Kodama is described as a politically connected figure who worked with the CIA after WWII. Hosts discuss Japanese anti-organized crime laws resembling RICO, the yakuza's enduring income, and yakuza films such as Battles Without Honor and Humanity and Black Rain.

segments.title: Tattoos and bathhouses
segments.summary: Chuck describes Japanese bathhouses that have tattoo restrictions, tied to yakuza association with tattoos.

segments.title: Listener mail: video blog plug and social media
segments.summary: A listener email announces a video blog and reflects on the show's history, followed by hosts giving their Facebook and Twitter handles and an email address.
